\section{The question we are trying to answer}


In this report we ask a narrow question. After qualifying, and before the race starts, can we tell which drivers will finish in the top three? We use the Formula 1 World Championship tables from 1950 to 2024. The prediction cutoff matters. Anything that is only known once the race is underway, such as the finishing order, the points scored that day, the retirement reason, the pit stops, or the fastest lap, is not allowed into the model as an input for that same race.


The cleaned table has 25,302 driver-race rows, and 13.4\% of them are podiums. That rate is the reason we do not treat every metric as equal. A ranking that ignores the features would score a PR-AUC near 0.134 on the full table, and near 0.150 on the 2022-2024 seasons, because that is simply the share of positive rows. ROC-AUC answers a different question: if we pick one driver who podiumed and one who did not, how often does the model give the podium driver the higher probability? A coin-flip ranking sits near 0.500. We use PR-AUC as the main score and ROC-AUC as the secondary score. F1, precision, and recall are reported at one cutoff, and that cutoff is chosen only on 2020-2021.


\begin{takeaway}
\textbf{Takeaway.} The rest of the report follows that cutoff. First we check that the tables join cleanly and that the label is one row per driver per race. Then we answer three descriptive questions about front-row starts, home races, and mechanical retirements. Only after that do we train models, and we judge them by whether they rank the rare podium rows above the rest.
\end{takeaway}



\section{What we checked before trusting the joins}


The raw files are the 14 Kaggle/Ergast tables, and we do not edit them. The literal value \textbackslash{}N is read as missing. Dates are parsed as dates, and qualifying times such as 1:25.187 are converted to seconds. We then audited the keys that the later joins depend on.


Table 1 covers all fourteen supplied tables, including composite keys for lap times and pit stops. Together they hold 701,433 rows. Every audited key is non-null, and none of these keys is duplicated. That is the check we needed before treating circuitId, driverId, raceId, and the other identifiers as safe join keys.

The results file has 26,759 rows, but it is not yet one row per driver per race. Early shared drives produce more than one result for the same driver in the same race. We found 85 such driver-race groups. The rule we keep is deterministic: prefer the row with a real grid start (grid greater than 0), then the better finishing position, then the smaller resultId. After that rule, 26,668 rows remain and each pair (raceId, driverId) appears once.


The second step removes drivers who did not enter the race. A result row with finishing code F belongs to a driver who did not qualify, did not prequalify, or failed the 107\% rule. That is settled before the race starts, and the instructor ruled that these rows may be removed. We remove 1,366 of them before any feature is built, so a skipped weekend never counts as a race in a driver's form window or in the size of the field. Withdrawals (code W) stay: that code is only known after the race, and a grid of 0 can also be a real pit-lane start. 25,302 rows remain, and the seasons run from 1950 to 2024.


Grid position 0 is not a better starting spot than pole. It accounts for 6.1\% of rows before the F rows are removed and 1.1\% after. We keep it as a flag and treat the numeric grid position as missing in those rows, so the model cannot learn that 0 is the front of the field.

Resolving shared drives removes 91 extra rows. Duplicate participation falls from 176 rows to zero, while the podium rate moves only from 12.69\% to 12.73\% and the median non-zero grid remains 12.0. So we fix the prediction grain without materially reshaping the label or the starting-position distribution. Removing the F rows takes out 1,366 more rows, and none of them is a podium, so the podium rate rises to 13.42\%. That rise is arithmetic, not a change in what a podium means: a driver who never raced cannot finish in the top three. The grid-0 share falls from 6.1\% to 1.1\%.


\begin{takeaway}
\textbf{Takeaway.} The joins we rely on later are supported by the key audit, and the modelling grain is one driver in one race who actually entered it. The cleaning choices are recorded so that a shared drive cannot silently become two training rows and a driver who never raced cannot become a row of zeros.
\end{takeaway}



\section{Qualifying coverage is not stable across history}


Qualifying position is an obvious pre-race feature, but it is not recorded for most of the early championship. Figure 3 plots, for each season, the share of driver-race rows that have a qualifying position. We use this plot to decide whether we can drop seasons that lack qualifying, or whether we have to keep a feature that survives the whole time span.


\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}
\begin{axis}[width=0.883\linewidth, height=5.2cm, xlabel={Season}, ylabel={Qualifying coverage}, ymin=0, ymax=1.05, xmin=1950, xmax=2024, ymajorgrids, scaled ticks=false, xtick distance=10]
\addplot[navy, thick] coordinates {(1950,0) (1951,0) (1952,0) (1953,0) (1954,0) (1955,0) (1956,0) (1957,0) (1958,0) (1959,0) (1960,0) (1961,0) (1962,0) (1963,0) (1964,0) (1965,0) (1966,0) (1967,0) (1968,0) (1969,0) (1970,0) (1971,0) (1972,0) (1973,0) (1974,0) (1975,0) (1976,0) (1977,0) (1978,0) (1979,0) (1980,0) (1981,0) (1982,0) (1983,0) (1984,0) (1985,0) (1986,0) (1987,0) (1988,0) (1989,0) (1990,0) (1991,0) (1992,0) (1993,0) (1994,0.935252) (1995,1) (1996,0.446483) (1997,0.588235) (1998,0.440922) (1999,0.185185) (2000,0.235925) (2001,0.0589812) (2002,0.117318) (2003,1) (2004,1) (2005,1) (2006,1) (2007,1) (2008,1) (2009,1) (2010,1) (2011,0.991189) (2012,0.991632) (2013,1) (2014,0.995086) (2015,0.989418) (2016,0.989177) (2017,0.995) (2018,1) (2019,0.995238) (2020,1) (2021,0.997727) (2022,1) (2023,1) (2024,1)};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Share of driver-race rows with a recorded qualifying position, by season. Coverage is essentially zero until the mid-1990s, unstable until 2003, and then close to complete.}
\end{figure}


In our modelling table, coverage is 0\% in 1950 and still 0\% in 1993. It jumps to 93.5\% in 1994 and 100\% in 1995, then falls again. The low point of that second gap is 5.9\% in 2001. From 2003 onwards the line sits on or next to 100\%, and 2024 is 100\%. Averaged over seasons, coverage is 7.2\% before 2000 and 89.4\% from 2000 on. At row level, 58.6\% of all driver-races have no qualifying position.


We observe two different regimes, not a smooth rise. The early championship has almost no qualifying rows in this snapshot. The seasons from 1994 to 2002 are patchy. The seasons we later use for validation and test are essentially complete. Dropping the early years would throw away most of the history, and it would also make the training set look more like the test set than it really is. We keep every season, store an explicit missingness flag, and treat grid position as the starting-order feature that exists throughout. The flag lets the model see that a qualifying value was absent, rather than hiding that fact inside a filled-in number.


\begin{takeaway}
\textbf{Takeaway.} Qualifying is a modern-era measurement in this dataset. Any model that depends on it alone would be fitting 2003-2024 and guessing before that. Grid position is the feature that can be compared across the whole 75 seasons.
\end{takeaway}



\section{Three questions about the races, before any model}


The prediction model comes later. These three questions use the joined tables directly. We separate what the counts show from what we are willing to infer. None of the three answers is a causal claim.



\subsection{Front-row starts convert to podiums much more often than other starts}


A front-row start means grid position 1 or 2 on the final grid. Recorded non-starters are removed from this descriptive denominator, even though withdrawals remain in the prediction table to respect the cutoff. We do not use qualifying position for this definition. A penalty can move a driver back between qualifying and the start, and the car that lines up first is the one we want. Results are joined to races and then to circuits. We split the history at 2014, the hybrid-era change, and we only rank a circuit inside an era when it has at least ten front-row starts there. That filter leaves 44 circuits in 1950-2013 and 19 circuits in 2014-2024.

2014-2024 & Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps & 81.8\% & 22 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}


We found a shift in the overall level, not just a different leading circuit. Across circuits that pass the ten-start rule, the median front-row podium rate is 56.8\% in 1950-2013 and 77.8\% in 2014-2024. The early range runs from 28.6\% at Detroit Street Circuit (14 starts) up to 80.6\% at Magny-Cours (36 starts). The modern range runs from 59.1\% at Hungaroring (22 starts) up to 88.9\% at Suzuka (18 starts).


If we ignore the circuit filter and use every front-row start in the modelling table, the rate is 56.1\% of 1,786 starts before 2014, and 76.0\% of 454 starts from 2014 on. The podium rate among all starters, not just the front row, is 13.3\% and 14.8\% in those same eras. A front-row car is several times more likely to podium than a typical starter. The modern front row converts at a higher rate than the historical front row, while the all-starter rate only moves from 13\% to 15\%.


The ranking itself needs a sample-size caution. Istanbul Park is second in the early list at 78.6\%, but that is 14 starts. Dijon-Prenois and Bremgarten sit near the top with 12 and 10 starts. Magny-Cours (36 starts) and Sepang (30 starts) are firmer early observations. The next early circuit, Suzuka, is also at 70\%, and it has 50 starts, so that rate is not carried only by Bremgarten. In 2014-2024 the leading circuits each have between 18 and 22 starts, so the order is less sensitive to one or two races, but Suzuka's 88.9\% is still 18 starts, not a long census. We can say the leaders change with the era. We cannot say that a circuit causes the conversion rate. The front row is already occupied by the fastest cars.


\begin{takeaway}
\textbf{Takeaway.} Where a driver starts dominates this descriptive cut. Era changes the level of front-row conversion, and the circuit ranking is real under our ten-start rule, with wide uncertainty on the circuits that barely meet it.
\end{takeaway}



\subsection{Once the grid band is fixed, home drivers do not podium more often}


The second question is whether drivers do better at a home race. We map nationality to a circuit country (British to the UK, Dutch to the Netherlands, and so on) and mark a row as home when those match. Drivers whose nationality is not in the map are left out. We then compare home and away podium rates inside the same grid bands, because Section 4.1 already shows that starting position can overwhelm a smaller effect. Figure 5 plots the two series.

Figure 6 and Table 5 mainly show the effect of the grid, not the passport. Away drivers podium 55.7\% of the time from positions 1-3 (3,055 starts), 26.4\% from 4-6, 9.6\% from 7-10, 3.1\% from 11-15, and 0.8\% from 16th or worse. Home drivers track those rates: 54.9\%, 24.7\%, 8.9\%, 3.4\%, and 0.8\%.


The home-minus-away gaps we measure are $-$0.8, $-$1.7, $-$0.7, +0.3, and $-$0.0 percentage points. Four of the five bands are slightly negative. The only positive gap is positions 11-15, and it is +0.3 percentage points.


Home samples are also much smaller. In the front band we have 264 home starts against 3,055 away starts, so a gap under one percentage point is not a stable difference. Compared with the drop from the front band (about 55\%) to the back band (under 1\%), the home contrast is small.


This suggests that a raw home-versus-away average would mostly pick up who starts near the front, not a separate home advantage. The stratification is a control, not a causal model. The nationality map also misses drivers we could not assign, and it cannot represent dual nationality. We report a descriptive result: inside a grid band, home drivers in this table do not show a consistent podium advantage.


As a stricter check, a Mantel-Haenszel comparison stratified by every exact grid slot gives a home-race odds ratio of 0.955. A race-cluster bootstrap gives a 95\% interval from 0.825 to 1.110. Because the interval includes 1, the adjusted evidence does not establish either a home advantage or disadvantage. This is an association, not a causal effect.


\begin{takeaway}
\textbf{Takeaway.} Starting position sorts podium rates into a steep ladder. Home status, measured this way, does not move a driver from one rung to another.
\end{takeaway}



\subsection{Mechanical retirement rates are lower in 2022-2024, and small teams sit at the top of each list}


The third question is which constructors retire with a mechanical failure, and whether that rate changed between 2014-2021 and 2022-2024. We join results to status and constructor. A start counts as mechanical only when the status text is on a fixed list of component failures: engine, gearbox, brakes, hydraulics, power unit, and the other documented part failures. Crashes, driver errors, disqualifications, and collisions are not on that list. Cars that did not start are removed from the denominator. Those statuses are Did not prequalify, Did not qualify, Did not start, Excluded, Withdrew. A constructor-era needs at least 20 starts to appear. The rate is mechanical retirements divided by starts, so a team that finishes races is in the denominator even when it rarely fails.


{\small The included statuses are: Alternator, Battery, Brake duct, Brakes, Clutch, Cooling system, Differential, Driveshaft, Drivetrain, ERS, Electrical, Electronics, Engine, Engine fire, Engine misfire, Exhaust, Fire, Front wing, Fuel leak, Fuel pressure, Fuel pump, Fuel system, Gearbox, Hydraulics, Mechanical, Oil leak, Oil pressure, Overheating, Power Unit, Power loss, Puncture, Radiator, Rear wing, Safety belt, Spark plugs, Steering, Suspension, Technical, Throttle, Transmission, Turbo, Tyre, Tyre puncture, Undertray, Vibrations, Water leak, Water pressure, Water pump, Wheel, Wheel bearing, Wheel nut. Rare wordings that are not on this list are counted as non-mechanical. That choice can miss an ambiguous failure, and it can also avoid treating a collision as a broken part. We would rather under-count borderline cases than inflate the rate. Engine fire and engine misfire are counted as mechanical because they are engine failures; heat shield fire is not counted. None of these statuses occur in 2014-2024, so this choice does not change the rates.\par}

Red Bull and McLaren are both at 3.7\% on 136 starts.


An interesting observation is the Alfa Romeo name across the cut: 4.2\% in 2014-2021 (5 of 120 starts) against 12.5\% in 2022-2024. The same constructor name does not mean the same car, and this table does not say why the rate rose. What the table does show is that the top of each era is a smaller or shorter-lived entry, while the large teams are clustered well below the leaders. The era totals are lower after 2021. One reading is the 2022 regulation change. The status strings and the 20-start filter can also move the rate, so we stop at the comparison.


\begin{takeaway}
\textbf{Takeaway.} Mechanical retirements, under this definition, are less common in 2022-2024 than in 2014-2021. The identity of the highest-rate constructor changes, and those leading rates rest on fewer starts than the works teams.
\end{takeaway}



\section{What the model is allowed to see}


The descriptive results above already point at the grid. The modelling step has to respect the cutoff. We build 16 inputs in five groups. Form uses a shift before the rolling window, so today's result is not inside today's features. Constructor form is averaged across both cars first, so one teammate cannot see the other teammate's result from the same race. Championship points and rank are taken from the previous race in the same season, because a standings row describes the table after a race. Before a driver's or team's first race of a season nothing has been scored yet, so points and rank are set to 0 there. Form before a driver's first race has no history, and we leave it missing rather than filling it with the future.


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Feature groups. Post-race position, points scored today, laps, status, pit stops, and fastest lap are excluded.}
{\small\rowcolors{2}{white}{zebra}
\begin{tabular}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{\dimexpr(\linewidth-6\tabcolsep)*168/1000\relax}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{\dimexpr(\linewidth-6\tabcolsep)*460/1000\relax}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{\dimexpr(\linewidth-6\tabcolsep)*372/1000\relax}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{navy}
\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Group}} & \textcolor{white}{\textbf{Inputs}} & \textcolor{white}{\textbf{Why it is known before the start}} \\
\midrule
Grid & Grid position, pit-lane flag, front-row flag, field size & Final grid is set before lights out \\
Qualifying & Position, best Q1/Q2/Q3 time, missingness flag & Qualifying is already finished \\
Form & Driver and constructor podium rate over the previous 5 races, prior starts & Current race is shifted out \\
Standings & Driver and constructor points and rank & Attached from the previous race only \\
Context & Driver age, year & Known on race morning \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}


We split by season, not at random. A random split would let 2023 teach the model about 2022. Training is every season through 2019, validation is 2020-2021, and the test seasons 2022-2024 are scored once. Training fits the imputer, scaler, and weights; validation makes every choice (preprocessing, ablation, model, cutoff); test is only reported. Table 9 shows why that split is not a copy of the same problem three times.

Our training seasons have 23,163 rows and 1,018 races, but 64.0\% of those rows have no qualifying result. Validation has only 780 rows and 39 races, and the test set has 1,359 rows and 68 races. That matches the field size: training averages 22.8 starters per race, against 20.0 in validation. There are still three podium places, shared across fewer cars.


All 7 of our split checks pass: every row is assigned once, no race appears in two splits, and the last training race is before the first validation race, which is before the first test race. Figure 8 shows the split on the season axis together with the two quantities that drift across it.

To check our choice, Table 10 holds out the same number of rows three ways, and we train the logistic baseline on the rest. With a random-row split, 100.0\% of held-out rows have their own race in training, and 98.2\% have later seasons in training. A random-race split removes the first problem but not the second. The chronological split has zero of both. Random hold-outs also mix every era, so their score (0.588 PR-AUC for random rows, against 0.730 on 2020-2021) answers a different question from predicting the next seasons.

From these results, we notice that validation is a short window. Two seasons and 39 races can separate a large gap from a small one, but they cannot support a fine ranking of models that differ by a few thousandths. We still use it for the decisions the test set must not make: the probability cutoff, and which model is used in the examples.


\begin{takeaway}
\textbf{Takeaway.} The features are pre-race by construction, and the split is chronological. The training years are a different problem from 2020-2024: more missing qualifying, larger fields, and a lower podium rate.
\end{takeaway}



\subsection{Sprint races: known before the start, but not a feature}


A sprint is a separate short race on the same weekend, stored in the sprint-results table. We had to decide whether it leaks. By time it does not: every sprint ends one day before the main race, so its result is known before the lights go out. We still leave it out, for two reasons. Sprints exist only from 2021, so no training row (1950-2019) has one; there are 0 such rows. And in 2021-2022 the sprint set the main-race grid, so the grid features already contain it (Table 11).

In 2023-2024 the sprint stopped setting the grid, which follows qualifying again. A sprint feature would then cover only 12 weekends, so we leave it out. The hazard we guard against is a join: sprint positions and points sit under the same race identifier as the main race, but they belong to a different race. Standings are already moved to the following round, so sprint points reach the features only through the previous round.



\subsection{Drivers who did not enter the race}


Before this step 6.1\% of rows have grid 0, and the feature name suggests a pit-lane start. Most of them were not. 1,366 rows are drivers who did not qualify, did not prequalify, or failed the 107\% rule. All of them are in 1952-2012, all are in training, and none finished on the podium. Only 87 grid-0 rows are real pit-lane or exceptional starts (Table 12). The instructor ruled that these F rows are known before the race and may be removed, and that withdrawals may not, so we remove the first and keep the second.

We scored the decision on the same validation seasons. Keeping the F rows instead changes validation PR-AUC by $-$0.0005 for logistic regression and +0.0144 for the network. Keeping them in the history but dropping them from the training rows only changes it by $-$0.0001 and +0.0126. Logistic regression, which has no random seed, moves by at most 0.0005. The network moves by up to 0.0144, but one network seed can sit 0.021 away from its own three-seed average (Section 5.4), so the network cannot separate these options. The choice rests on the ruling and on what a row means, not on a score. Removing the withdrawals as well, which the ruling does not allow, would change the network by +0.0182. Validation and test contain no F rows, so the same rows are scored either way. The pit-lane flag now marks 289 rows, 202 withdrawals with grid 0 and 87 drivers who raced from the pit lane or an exceptional start. It is no longer a did-not-qualify marker, but it is still not a pure pit-lane flag.



\subsection{Evidence for each individual feature}


The group-level ablation in Section 8 says what a whole group adds to the model. Each feature also has its own exploratory evidence, computed on the training seasons only (Table 13 and Figure 9). For every feature we report the share of missing cells, the podium rate in its lowest and highest bin, and a one-feature ROC-AUC. An AUC above 0.5 means a higher value goes with more podiums, and below 0.5 the reverse. The same AUC on validation checks that the pattern still holds in later seasons.

\textbf{Strong single signals.} Position features carry the most. Qualifying position has an AUC of 0.09 (lower is better, measured on the 36\% of rows that have it) and grid position 0.12; the podium rate falls from 47\% (grid) and 52\% (qualifying) in the best bin to 0.5\% and 0.7\% in the worst. The standings ranks (0.27 and 0.26), the form rates (0.81 and 0.83), and the points (0.76 and 0.72) come next. The front-row flag (0.67) and prior starts (0.66) are clear but smaller. All of these keep their direction on validation, with similar or slightly stronger AUCs.


\textbf{Weak single signals, kept for another reason.} Field size (0.45), driver age (0.55), qualifying time (0.45), the pit-lane flag (0.49), and the qualifying-missing flag (0.49) are close to 0.5 on their own. A raw qualifying time is not comparable across circuits and eras, so it says little without the rest of the row. The two flags are indicators. Removing the qualifying-missing flag changes PR-AUC only slightly (Section 6.4), but the flag records which rows were imputed, and rows with no grid position (withdrawals and pit-lane starts) never podium, while rows with no qualifying record podium at about the average rate (12.9\% against 13.4\%). Year (0.50) has essentially no single-feature signal, and field size and year are flat or constant on validation, where every race has 20 starters. The ablation shows the whole context group adds the least of the five (0.001 PR-AUC). Section 5.4 tests the two calendar features one at a time: year is kept and round was removed.


\begin{takeaway}
\textbf{What this does and does not show.} A one-feature AUC ignores the other 15 features. A feature that looks weak here can still help in combination, and a strong one can add little once the grid is present: the ablation shows qualifying adds only 0.006 on top of the grid. The AUCs describe association in past races, not causes.
\end{takeaway}



\subsection{Calendar features: keep year, remove round}


Year and round were added as context: the era and the point in the season. On their own neither separates podiums from the rest (year has a single-feature AUC of 0.50), so we tested each one inside the full models. Every variant is trained on 1950-2019 and scored on 2020-2021 only, and the network is averaged over three seeds (Table 14).

\midrule
used (no round) & Logistic regression & 16 & 0.7301 & 0.0000 & 0.7301 & +0.0000 \\
used (no round) & Random forest & 16 & 0.7175 & 0.0000 & 0.7175 & +0.0000 \\
used (no round) & Shallow neural network & 16 & 0.7228 & 0.0052 & 0.7166 & +0.0000 \\
put round back & Logistic regression & 17 & 0.7293 & 0.0000 & 0.7293 & $-$0.0008 \\
put round back & Random forest & 17 & 0.7139 & 0.0000 & 0.7139 & $-$0.0036 \\
put round back & Shallow neural network & 17 & 0.7232 & 0.0170 & 0.7443 & +0.0003 \\
also remove year & Logistic regression & 15 & 0.7307 & 0.0000 & 0.7307 & +0.0006 \\
also remove year & Random forest & 15 & 0.7052 & 0.0000 & 0.7052 & $-$0.0123 \\
also remove year & Shallow neural network & 15 & 0.7017 & 0.0157 & 0.7108 & $-$0.0212 \\
round back, year removed & Logistic regression & 16 & 0.7289 & 0.0000 & 0.7289 & $-$0.0012 \\
round back, year removed & Random forest & 16 & 0.7100 & 0.0000 & 0.7100 & $-$0.0074 \\
round back, year removed & Shallow neural network & 16 & 0.6869 & 0.0446 & 0.7167 & $-$0.0360 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}


\textbf{Round adds nothing, so we removed it.} Putting round back changes validation PR-AUC by $-$0.0008 for logistic regression, which has no random seed, by $-$0.0036 for the forest, and by +0.0003 for the network, far inside the noise of a three-seed average (about 0.010). None of these comes close to a real effect such as removing year ($-$0.0212 for the network), and they do not agree in direction. The standings already carry the same information, because points and rank build up race by race. Round also changes meaning across eras: a season had about 8 races in the 1950s and 24 in 2024, so round 8 was a finale then and an early race now. With no measurable gain and an unstable meaning, the simpler model wins.


\textbf{Year helps, so we kept it.} Removing year changes the score by +0.0006 for logistic regression, $-$0.0123 for the forest and $-$0.0212 for the network. The network loses the most of the three models, about 2 times the noise of a three-seed average (about 0.010). The same test inside the old 17-feature model, with round still there, gives $-$0.0004, $-$0.0038 and $-$0.0363, so year helps the nonlinear models with or without round. That old model without year is also unstable: its network seed spread is 0.045. Year alone says nothing, but together with grid and form it lets the nonlinear models adjust for the era: larger fields, worse reliability, and missing qualifying in older seasons. One caveat: the test seasons lie outside the training years, so the models must extrapolate year, and a tree cannot, so the forest treats 2022 like 2019.


\begin{takeaway}
\textbf{Takeaway.} One seed is not enough to rank the models. With round, the network's seed-42 score was 0.7443, 0.021 above its own three-seed average of 0.7232. Without round, seed 42 scores 0.7166 and the average is 0.7228. The average barely moved, yet the single seed fell, and that alone moved the network from first to below logistic regression in Section 7. We therefore read single-seed network differences of about 0.021 as noise throughout this report.
\end{takeaway}



\section{Feature engineering and preprocessing: strategy, effect on the values, and order}


Missing qualifying, grid, and form values have to be filled inside the model pipeline, using training rows only. We compare three settings of logistic regression on the validation seasons: median imputation with scaling, median imputation without scaling, and filling missing values with zero before scaling. The test seasons are not used for this choice.


\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Preprocessing comparison for logistic regression on 2020-2021 only.}
{\small\rowcolors{2}{white}{zebra}
\begin{tabular}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{\dimexpr(\linewidth-6\tabcolsep)*366/1000\relax}>{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{\dimexpr(\linewidth-6\tabcolsep)*321/1000\relax}>{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{\dimexpr(\linewidth-6\tabcolsep)*313/1000\relax}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{navy}
\textcolor{white}{\textbf{Preprocessing}} & \textcolor{white}{\textbf{Validation ROC-AUC}} & \textcolor{white}{\textbf{Validation PR-AUC}} \\
\midrule
median + scaling & 0.926 & 0.730 \\
median, no scaling & 0.925 & 0.731 \\
zero + scaling & 0.927 & 0.726 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}


We can see that the three PR-AUC values sit between 0.726 and 0.731. The gap is 0.005. Median imputation with scaling is the best of the three on the metric we care about. Zero-filling with scaling is slightly higher on ROC-AUC (0.927 against 0.926). If we had followed ROC-AUC, we would have picked a different setting. The difference is small enough that we do not treat preprocessing as the main lever. We keep median imputation with scaling for the linear model and the network. The forest does not use scaling, because a tree split does not depend on the units of a feature.



\subsection{What feature engineering does to the values}


In Table 16 we compare each raw source column with the feature we built from it. Raw grid has a minimum of 0 and 1.1\% zeros, which would rank a pit-lane start ahead of pole. In the grid-position feature those zeros become missing, so the minimum is 1, and the pit-lane flag carries the information instead. Qualifying strings become seconds; after the join to every driver-race row, 59.2\% of rows have no qualifying time. Shifted form is missing on a driver's first race, because nothing earlier exists, and that gap is what the imputer fills next. Previous-race standings are not imputed. Before a driver's or team's first race of a season they used to be empty, and the median imputer filled them with about 3 points and rank 13, points nobody had scored. They are now set to 0 points and rank 0. Extra flags marking these rows gave no validation gain, so no flags were added.

\subsection{What imputation and scaling do to the values}


In Table 17 we measure both steps on the training rows. Median imputation writes the training median into every gap. It does not change the range, because the median is inside it, but it piles rows onto one value and shrinks the spread. qualifying\_time\_seconds is missing in 64.5\% of training rows, and its standard deviation falls by 40.3\%. The qualifying-missing flag keeps the fact that a value was filled. Scaling then puts every training feature at mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Raw ranges run from 0-1 for the flags to 722 constructor points; after scaling they share one scale, so neither the logistic penalty nor the network's gradient steps are dominated by large units. Scaling is linear, so the shape and order of values do not change.

\subsection{Preprocessing-order experiments}


The table above changes which strategy we use. We also ran three experiments that change the \textit{order} of the steps (Table 18), each scored on validation with logistic regression and the network. A swaps median imputation and scaling. B swaps zero-filling and scaling. C fits the preprocessing on all seasons before splitting, against the normal fit on training only.

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}


\textbf{A.} Median imputation commutes with a linear rescale, so a missing grid becomes 12.0 either way. Only the scaler's statistics differ, because scaling first measures spread on observed values. Validation PR-AUC moves by +0.0000 for logistic regression and +0.0164 for the network. \textbf{B.} Here order changes the value. Zero-filling first writes a literal 0, a grid slot ahead of pole and a 0-second lap. Zero-filling after scaling writes the training mean (12.0 for grid). Validation PR-AUC changes by +0.0043 (logistic) and $-$0.0054 (network). \textbf{C.} Fitting before the split lets 2020-2024 set the medians and scaling used in training. The score moves by +0.0001 and +0.0208; small or not, it uses future data, so we never do it.


\begin{takeaway}
\textbf{Takeaway.} We keep split, then median imputation, then scaling, all fitted on training rows inside the model pipeline. Logistic regression is almost indifferent to strategy and order (every change is within 0.005 PR-AUC). The network moves by up to 0.021, about the 0.021 that one seed can move on its own (Section 5.4), so its numbers cannot rank the orders either. We fix the order on principle: fit on training rows only, and impute before scaling so the scaler sees the filled values. The next sections test which information the models need.
\end{takeaway}



\subsection{Missing values: impute, drop columns, or drop rows?}


About 64\% of training rows have no qualifying record, so we did not choose the handling by preference. Each approach is scored on the same validation seasons (Table 19). The network is run once with one seed, and one seed can sit 0.021 away from its own average (Section 5.4), so network differences of that size are noise. We decide on logistic regression, the selected model, because it has no random seed.

For logistic regression every alternative stays within 0.006 of median imputation (the best alternative, drop training rows with any missing feature, is +0.0014). For the network, mean imputation changes the score by $-$0.010, k-nearest-neighbour imputation by +0.016, and iterative imputation by +0.017. Dropping the two sparse qualifying columns changes the network by $-$0.030, the one network change clearly beyond single-seed noise, and removing the missing-value flag instead changes it by $-$0.005. Dropping rows keeps only 8,348 or 8,054 of 23,163 training rows and changes the scores by $-$0.001 and +0.001 for logistic regression, $-$0.011 and +0.022 for the network. \textbf{We keep median imputation with the flag}, fitted on training rows only: for logistic regression it is tied with every alternative, the network's single-seed numbers cannot rank them, and it keeps all the history.



\section{Three models, and why the scores are not interchangeable}


We fit three classifiers on the same training rows and the same 16 features. Logistic regression is the linear baseline, with class weights so the rare podium rows are not ignored. The random forest has 240 trees, a depth limit of 12, and a minimum of 30 rows per leaf; it can use combinations such as a strong recent record together with a poor grid. The neural network has two hidden layers, of 32 and 12 units. Each model's settings were searched on validation (Section 7.1), and the probability cutoff that maximises F1 on validation is chosen last. That produces a different cutoff for each model, because the three probability scales are not the same number line. A cutoff of 0.455 on the network is not automatically more aggressive than 0.625 on the logistic model. Precision and recall tell us what the cutoff actually does.


Figure 12 compares the three models on the test seasons only. Table 20 gives training, validation, and test, so we can see whether a high training score survives.

On the test set we measure a ROC-AUC of 0.935 for logistic regression, 0.937 for the forest, and 0.933 for the network. Those three numbers are within 0.005 of each other. In the pair reading of ROC-AUC, a true podium finisher outranks a non-podium about 93 to 94 times out of 100. That is a strong ranking. It is also a ranking on which the models do not separate. ROC-AUC compresses the comparison because most rows are not podiums, so a modest number of false alarms barely moves the false-positive rate.


PR-AUC is where they separate a little. On test, the forest scores 0.717, the network 0.716, and logistic regression 0.702. The test podium rate is 15.0\%, so a useless ranking would sit near 0.150. All three models are far above that floor. The forest's lead over logistic regression is 0.015 PR-AUC. We call that a small lead, not a different kind of model. We selected logistic regression before looking at this comparison, because its validation PR-AUC of 0.730 was ahead of 0.717 for the network and 0.717 for the forest. It also leads on the three-seed average (Section 7.1), so the choice does not rest on one seed. The test seasons are never used to choose.


The operating points we chose explain the precision and recall bars in Figure 12. At its validation cutoff, logistic regression has test precision 0.529 and recall 0.892. It catches most podiums and accepts more false alarms. The forest has precision 0.662 and recall 0.652, and the network has precision 0.720 and recall 0.554. The network is the conservative one of the three. Test F1 ends up almost tied, from 0.626 to 0.664. Same F1, different mix of missed podiums and false podiums.


The training column is the check for memorizing. All three models have a training PR-AUC below their validation score: 0.562 for logistic regression, 0.646 for the forest, and 0.576 for the network. That was not true of the first forest, which scored 0.918 on training and 0.696 on validation because it had no depth limit and four rows per leaf. The validation search in Section 7.1 limited it. We do not read the higher validation score as the model improving after 2019. Training has a lower podium rate and far more missing qualifying, so the PR-AUC floor on training is lower as well. The comparison we trust is validation against test, where the positive rate is almost the same.


\begin{takeaway}
\textbf{Takeaway.} All three models rank podium finishers well above non-podiums. On the primary score, logistic regression is slightly ahead on validation and slightly behind on test, and both gaps are smaller than the uncertainty of the race samples (Section 7.2). ROC-AUC hides even that difference.
\end{takeaway}



\subsection{Searching each model's settings, on validation only}


We trained each model on 1950-2019 and scored it on 2020-2021 for every setting in a small grid. Our grid held 8 settings for logistic regression, 9 for the forest, and 12 for the network. We averaged the network over three seeds because its score depends on the initialisation. We did not use the test seasons (Table 21).

\textbf{Random forest: improved.} The starting forest (no depth limit, 4 rows per leaf) ranked 6th of 9. It scored 0.696 on validation but 0.918 on training, a memorised fit. A depth limit of 12 with 30 rows per leaf scores 0.717 and ranks 1st of 9. The best setting (max\_depth: 12, min\_samples\_leaf: 30) is only 0.000 higher, far inside the validation noise in Section 7.2, so we keep the depth limit as the more constrained model. It cuts the training score to 0.646, so it no longer memorizes the training seasons. No test season took part in the choice. \textbf{Shallow network: a noisy search.} One layer of 8, 16, 32, or 64 units and two layers of 32 and 12 or 64 and 32, each with two regularization strengths, were all tried and averaged over three seeds. The adopted two layers of 32 and 12 with alpha 0.02 score 0.7228 and rank 7th of 12, against 0.7179 for the starting alpha of 0.002. The best setting (hidden\_layer\_sizes: (64,), alpha: 0.002) is 0.013 higher, while one setting's seed spread reaches 0.025 in this search. The ranking is also unstable: with round in the features, the adopted setting ranked first. Picking the top of a ranking that moves with one input and one seed would be picking noise, so we keep the adopted network. Networks with 8 units are clearly worse, so it is not a deliberately weak choice. Its three-seed average is still below logistic regression's 0.7301. \textbf{Logistic regression} is insensitive: L1 and L2 penalties and C from 0.01 to 10 all fall between 0.710 and 0.730, and the starting C = 1 with L2 ties for best (within 0.0005), so we kept it.



\subsection{How much the validation score can be trusted}

The full model sits at 0.730. Dropping the grid group costs 0.025 PR-AUC, the largest loss. Standings are next, at 0.017. Form, qualifying, and context cost 0.016, 0.006, and 0.001. The qualifying drop is small once the grid is already in the model. That fits the sport and the earlier definition: the published grid already contains qualifying order, plus any penalty. We do not conclude that qualifying is irrelevant on its own. We conclude that, next to the grid, it is mostly repeated information.


ROC-AUC barely notices the same deletion. It moves from 0.926 to 0.920 when the grid group is removed. This is the same lesson as the model comparison we drew in Section 7. A metric that stays high while the primary score drops is a poor guide for what to keep.


The context and qualifying changes are about the same size as the logistic-regression preprocessing gaps in Section 6. On 39 validation races, we treat those as small. The grid drop is several times larger, and it agrees with the descriptive ladder in Section 4.2, where podium rate falls from about 55\% at the front of the grid to under 1\% at the back.


\begin{takeaway}
\textbf{Takeaway.} For the linear model, the final grid is the group we cannot remove without a visible loss. Recent standings help. Qualifying, form, and calendar context add less once the grid is present.
\end{takeaway}



\section{What the selected model relies on, with forest cross-checks}


Logistic regression is the selected model, so we first explain it directly through its standardized coefficients and an exact local log-odds decomposition. We then retain permutation importance, SHAP, and LIME as separate checks on the random forest. Tree explanations apply directly to the forest; we do not borrow them as an account of logistic regression. Permutation importance shuffles one validation column at a time and measures the drop in PR-AUC. Global SHAP averages the size of each feature's push across 400 validation rows. Local SHAP is one of those rows. A positive value pushes that row toward a podium relative to the forest's background. A negative value pushes it away. These are associations inside the fitted forest. They are not estimates of what would happen if we moved a driver up the grid.

constructor\_podium\_rate\_5 & 0.065 \\
constructor\_rank\_before & 0.041 \\
driver\_rank\_before & 0.037 \\
year & 0.034 \\
front\_row & 0.027 \\
qualifying\_position & 0.020 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}


Global SHAP also puts grid position first, at 0.140, and constructor podium rate second (0.065), the same top two as permutation importance. Driver podium rate follows at 0.070. The two methods differ below that. Year has a mean SHAP value of 0.034 (rank 6) but a permutation importance of +0.000, and driver points before the race is the reverse: rank 6 under permutation and rank 9 under SHAP. A reasonable reading is that year, form, and the standings overlap with each other and with the grid. The trees use them, but once the other columns are left intact, destroying one of them alone does not collapse the score. We treat the shared finding as the reliable one: grid position first, constructor form second.


Figure 18 is one validation row from that sample, not a row we picked because it looks tidy. It is George Russell, Williams, 2021 Dutch Grand Prix. He qualified and started 11th in a field of 20, sat 15th in the championship, and had a podium in one of his previous five starts (driver podium rate 0.2). He did not podium.

\subsection{Local LIME explanation}


LIME provides the required model-agnostic local explanation for the same fixed validation case. We create 5,000 nearby records by either retaining each observed feature or replacing it with a value drawn from the training seasons. The random forest scores those records, and a distance-weighted ridge model approximates the forest around the explained row. A positive coefficient pushes the local surrogate toward a podium; a negative coefficient pushes it away.

The weighted local R-squared is only 0.203. This is low local fidelity: the linear surrogate captures only a small share of the forest's variation in the sampled neighbourhood. The displayed coefficients are therefore weak, unstable local evidence and must not be treated as a faithful decomposition or as global effects.


\begin{takeaway}
\textbf{Takeaway.} Grid position is the feature the explanation methods agree on, with constructor form second under both. They differ on the smaller features, such as year and driver points, which is what we expect when form, standings, and year overlap with the grid. None of these values is a causal effect of starting further forward.
\end{takeaway}



\section{Two predictions from the selected model}


The examples use the selected model, logistic regression, because it had the best validation PR-AUC. Its frozen cutoff is 0.625. Missing inputs are filled by the imputer that was fit on the training years. We show one complete historical row and one partial record that was never a real entry.


The complete row is Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes, 2022 Bahrain Grand Prix, round 1. He qualified 5th and started 5th in a field of 20. His previous five starts in this table were all podiums (driver rate 1.0) and the constructor's recent podium rate was 0.7. Because it is the first race of the season, his and Mercedes' championship points and rank are both 0. Logistic regression gives this row a podium probability of 0.906. That is above 0.625, so the predicted label is a podium. The actual result was third, a podium, so the prediction is correct. A fifth-place start and a perfect recent podium run were enough to lift the probability over the cutoff. The row is picked automatically as the first complete 2022 row. Before the round-1 standings fix, round-1 rows had empty standings and were skipped, so the example used to be the 2022 Saudi Arabian Grand Prix.


The partial record supplies only what we chose to type in: grid position 3, not a pit-lane start, not a front-row start, a field of 20, and season 2024. Every other feature is missing and is replaced with the training median. The API now returns the exact list and warns that 11 of 16 inputs were imputed. Logistic regression returns 0.387, below the cutoff, so the predicted label is not a podium. This record has no true result, because it is not a driver who started a race.


We should not read 0.387 as the historical podium rate of cars that start third. Section 4.2 puts that rate near 55\% for grid positions 1-3. The partial row is a third-place start glued onto a median historical driver, and the median driver in a 1950-2019 training set is not a podium contender. The low probability is what this imputer does with a half-empty row. It is evidence that the function accepts missing fields. It is not evidence about the front of the grid.


\begin{takeaway}
\textbf{Takeaway.} On a real 2022 row, the selected model correctly predicted a podium for a fifth-place start backed by a perfect recent podium run. On a synthetic partial row, the number is an imputed profile, and we do not interpret it as a base rate.
\end{takeaway}



\section{What we do not want the results to be taken to say}


Qualifying coverage is a property of this snapshot. We described it, and we kept a missingness flag, but we cannot tell from the chart alone how much of the pre-1994 gap is history and how much is the way the public tables were filled.


Constructor form is built per constructor identifier, and a renamed team usually gets a new one, so its form starts empty: Toro Rosso became AlphaTauri in 2020, Renault became Alpine in 2021, and AlphaTauri became RB in 2024. A few old identifiers are also reused years later, so Aston Martin in 2021 is linked to the unrelated 1959-1960 Aston Martin. Standings restart every season and driver form follows the driver, so only constructor form is touched, and only in the first five races of such a season: 30 of 780 validation rows and 20 of 1,359 test rows. None of them is a podium, and their constructor form is 0 or empty, which the imputer fills with the training median of 0. We keep the identifiers as they are rather than hand-map renames, because each link is a judgement (a rebrand is not the same as a sale to a new owner), and the evaluation would barely move.


The home analysis depends on a nationality-to-country map. Drivers we could not map are excluded, and drivers with more than one sporting nationality are forced into one label. The small home samples in the front of the grid mean a one-point gap is not something we would defend as a precise estimate.


The mechanical list is a rule we wrote down, not a measurement from the car. Ambiguous statuses can fall outside it. Leading rates such as Caterham's rest on a few dozen starts. The lower 2022-2024 totals are consistent with a more reliable field, and they are also consistent with changes in how retirements were described.


Validation is 39 races. We used it to pick a cutoff and a model, which is what a held-out test set requires, and we do not pretend it can rank effects of a few thousandths. A bootstrap over those races gives each PR-AUC an interval about 0.2 wide, and the differences between the models fall inside it. On the unseen test seasons PR-AUC is 0.702 for logistic regression, 0.717 for the forest and 0.716 for the network. Logistic regression is 0.013 behind, but a bootstrap over the 68 test races puts both differences from it inside an interval that includes zero (Section 7.2). We do not claim that the more complex models are better. We treat the three as tied in ranking quality and keep logistic regression as the readable baseline. Regulation changes in 2014 and 2022 sit inside the eras we compared. The models are associating historical patterns. They do not tell a team what would happen if it started one place further forward, and a probability is not a guarantee about the next race.



\section{What the evidence supports}


The tables join, and after 85 shared-drive groups are resolved and 1,366 did-not-enter rows are removed we have one row per driver per race, 25,302 of them, with a podium rate of 13.4\%. Qualifying is missing for most of the early history and nearly complete from 2003, so the grid is the starting-order feature we can actually follow from 1950.


Descriptively, front-row cars podium far more often than the field, and more often again after 2013. Home nationality, inside a grid band, does not produce a consistent extra podium rate. Mechanical retirement rates, on our component list and among teams with at least 20 starts, are lower in 2022-2024 than in 2014-2021, and the highest rates belong to shorter entries.


For prediction, logistic regression, a random forest, and a shallow network all clear the PR-AUC baseline of the recent seasons by a wide margin. Logistic regression is the one we select from the validation scores, by seed 42 and by the three-seed average. The untouched test seasons put the forest and the network slightly ahead (0.717 and 0.716, against 0.702), but the three models are within bootstrap uncertainty of each other on both validation and test, so the simplest and most readable model is the one we keep. Ablation, permutation, and SHAP agree that grid position carries the prediction, and permutation and SHAP also agree that constructor form comes second. They differ on the smaller features, and we do not force them to agree. The Hamilton example fits this picture in one row: a fifth-place start backed by a recent run of podiums lifted him over the cutoff, and he finished third.



\section{Data source and course notes}


We used Vopani's Formula 1 World Championship (1950-2024) dataset on Kaggle, a relational CSV version of the Ergast Formula 1 data. We accessed it in October 2026: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/rohanrao/formula-1-world-championship-1950-2020.


We followed Piazza post @10 and the related TA feedback for the status rules. Tyre, puncture, tyre puncture, fire, and safety belt count as mechanical failures; refuelling does not. We removed positionText F rows before feature construction and kept W rows. Since the Piazza export is not in the repository, we included the stricter mechanical-failure sensitivity check shown earlier.
